---
title: "How to tune feature computation"
---

Everything on this page applies to **every** calculator —
[SpikeGLX](compute-features-spikeglx.qmd), [NWB](compute-features-nwb.qmd),
[Zarr](compute-features-zarr.qmd), IBL PID, and the LF-only
[LFPack](load-lfp-features.qmd#computing-features-from-the-archives) and NumPy sources
alike. The
source-specific pages cover the usual call, `compute_denoised_features`; this one covers
controlling it: computing a single snippet, choosing the snippet windows, and changing how
each snippet is computed. The same `options` go to `compute_snippet` and to
`compute_denoised_features`, which applies them to every snippet.

## Compute a single snippet {#compute-a-single-snippet}

`compute_denoised_features` is built on a smaller call, `calc.compute_snippet(window,
options)`, which computes the features of one snippet from three objects:

1. A **calculator** — where the data comes from: any of the calculators above.
2. A **`SnippetWindow`** — which slice of time to compute over.
3. A **`FeatureComputationOptions`** — which feature families, where to write, and any
   per-feature parameters.

```python
from pathlib import Path

from ephysatlas.feature_calculators import FeatureComputationOptions, SnippetWindow

window = SnippetWindow(t_start=300.0, duration_ap=1.0, duration_lf=1.0)

options = FeatureComputationOptions(
    features_to_compute=["lf", "csd"],
    output_dir=Path("/data/features"),
)

result = calc.compute_snippet(window, options)   # calc: any calculator

print(result.features.shape)
print(result.computed_features)   # ('lf', 'csd')
```

To see the voltage this window covers, destriped as the features see it,
`calc.get_destriped_snippet(window)` returns it without computing any feature; see
[inspecting the destriped data](#inspecting-the-destriped-data).

### The snippet window

`SnippetWindow` sets one start time and **independent durations per band**:

| field | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `t_start` | `0.0` | Start time in seconds from the beginning of the recording |
| `duration_ap` | `5.0` | Length of the AP-band snippet, in seconds |
| `duration_lf` | `25.0` | Length of the LF-band snippet, in seconds |

The bands get different durations because they are informative on different timescales:
LF features want a long window to resolve low-frequency power, while AP/waveform features
are expensive and converge quickly. Setting a duration to `0.0` skips that band.

Start well after `t_start=0` — the first seconds of a recording often contain settling
artefacts. `300.0` is a common choice.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Start small

Features on a 1-second snippet of one probe take seconds; waveform features on a long
window take minutes to hours. Get the call working with `duration_ap=1.0`,
`duration_lf=1.0` and `features_to_compute=["lf"]` before scaling up.
:::

### Feature families

`features_to_compute` accepts any subset of four families:

| family | band | what it produces |
|---|---|---|
| `"lf"` | LF | Band power, RMS, spectral-decay parameters |
| `"csd"` | LF | The same measures on the current-source density |
| `"ap"` | AP | AP-band RMS and channel cross-correlation |
| `"waveforms"` | AP | Spike detection and waveform shape (needs `[full]`) |

Leave `features_to_compute=None` to compute every family the available bands support.
An unknown name raises `ValueError` listing the valid options.

See the [feature list reference](../reference/feature-list.qmd) for the exact columns each
family emits.

### What you get back

`compute_snippet` returns a `FeatureComputationResult`:

```python
result.features            # pd.DataFrame — one row per channel, with a `channel` column
result.computed_features   # families actually recalculated in this call
result.cached_features     # families loaded from existing files on disk
result.probe_level_dir     # .../features/<name>/
result.snippet_level_dir   # .../features/<name>/probe_<name>_<t_start>_<dur_ap>_<dur_lf>/
result.provenance          # versions + parameters stamped onto the written files
result.manifest_record     # one row for the aggregation step
```

`<name>` is the calculator's recording name, the `pid` of the aggregated table; each
calculator page gives its default.

### On-disk layout

With `output_dir` set, files are written in a two-level structure:

```text
/data/features/
└── subject42_probe00/                                      ← probe level (the `name`)
    ├── channels.pqt                                        channel metadata + geometry
    └── probe_subject42_probe00_000300.0_01.0_01.0/         ← snippet level
        ├── lf_features.pqt
        └── csd_features.pqt
```

The snippet directory name encodes `t_start`, `duration_ap` and `duration_lf`, so
different windows over the same recording sit side by side and never overwrite each other.
Each `*_features.pqt` carries the run's provenance in its `.attrs`.

Leave `output_dir=None` and nothing is written — `result.features` is returned in memory
and `probe_level_dir` / `snippet_level_dir` come back as `None`.

## Choose the snippet windows {#choose-the-snippet-windows}

`compute_denoised_features` draws the snippet start times for you. To choose them
yourself, draw the start times, then aggregate:

```python
from ephysatlas.feature_calculators import (
    SnippetWindow,
    compute_aggregated_features,
    get_snippet_start_times,
)

# seconds; a missing band has no duration
duration_s = min(d for d in calc.available_duration() if d is not None)
t_starts = get_snippet_start_times(
    duration_s, n_snippets=5, snippet_duration=5.0, margin=300.0
)
windows = [SnippetWindow(t, 5.0, 5.0) for t in t_starts]
df = compute_aggregated_features(calc, windows)
```

`margin` keeps the snippets away from both ends of the recording. `method="stratified"`
(the default) draws one random start in each of `n_snippets` equal bins, reproducibly
(`seed=0`); `method="linspace"` spaces them evenly.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Short recordings

`compute_denoised_features` keeps the default 5-minute margins, so a recording shorter
than 10 minutes plus one snippet raises `ValueError: Recording of ... s is too short for
300.0 s margins and 5.0 s snippets`.

Overlapping snippets raise `ValueError: Snippets starting at ... overlap` (or log a
warning with `on_overlap="warn"`). The stratified draw can place two starts closer than
one snippet when the usable range is short: with `margin=0`, three 5-second snippets fail
on a 20- or 25-second recording and fit on 30 seconds. On a short recording, draw the
times with `margin=0` and `method="linspace"`, and call `compute_aggregated_features`:

```python
t_starts = get_snippet_start_times(
    duration_s, n_snippets=3, snippet_duration=5.0, margin=0.0, method="linspace"
)
```
:::

### Write the snippets yourself {#write-the-snippets-yourself}

To keep every snippet on disk, and resume an interrupted run, loop over start times
reusing the calculator:

```python
output_dir = Path("/data/features")
options = FeatureComputationOptions(
    features_to_compute=["lf", "csd"],
    output_dir=output_dir,
    skip_saved_computation=True,   # resume instead of recomputing
)

results = []
for t_start in [300.0, 900.0, 1500.0, 2100.0]:
    window = SnippetWindow(t_start=t_start, duration_ap=1.0, duration_lf=1.0)
    result = calc.compute_snippet(window, options)
    print(t_start, result.computed_features, result.cached_features)
    results.append(result)
```

`skip_saved_computation=True` reuses feature files already present in the snippet
directory, so an interrupted run resumes where it stopped instead of starting over.

Then combine the snippets into one per-channel table, the one the models actually
consume. `aggregate_snippets` is the aggregation half of `compute_aggregated_features`;
it reads the snippet files back, so the snippets need an `output_dir`:

```python
from ephysatlas.feature_calculators import aggregate_snippets

df = aggregate_snippets(results)   # per-channel median, denoised, indexed by (pid, channel)
```

[Aggregate and denoise](aggregate-and-denoise.qmd) explains each step, and how to
aggregate snippets already on disk without the calculator.

## Computation options

`FeatureComputationOptions` controls one `compute_snippet` call. Every field has a working
default, so set only what you need to change.

### What to compute, and where it goes

| field | default | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `features_to_compute` | `None` | Families to compute: any of `"lf"`, `"csd"`, `"ap"`, `"waveforms"`. `None` computes everything the available bands support |
| `output_dir` | `None` | Root for the probe/snippet output tree. `None` writes nothing and returns features in memory only |
| `scratch_dir` | `None` | Scratch space for waveform extraction. `None` uses `dartsort/` in the system temp directory (`$TMPDIR`). Point this at a fast local disk when computing `waveforms`; a directory that cannot be created raises `OSError` |

### Caching and reruns

| field | default | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `skip_saved_computation` | `False` | Reuse feature files already in the snippet directory instead of recomputing them |
| `recompute_channels` | `False` | Rewrite `channels.pqt` even when it exists |
| `save_waveforms` | `False` | Persist the waveform arrays, not just the derived features |

`skip_saved_computation=True` is what makes a long multi-snippet run resumable. Which
families were reused is reported back:

```python
result = calc.compute_snippet(window, options)
print(result.computed_features)   # recalculated in this call
print(result.cached_features)     # loaded from disk
```

### Trajectory metadata

| field | default | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `include_trajectory` | `True` | Try to add `x_target` / `y_target` / `z_target` to the channel table |
| `require_trajectory` | `False` | Raise instead of continuing when that metadata is missing |

Only the IBL PID calculator, and a SpikeGLX calculator given a `traj_dict`, have a
trajectory to add. For every other source, leaving `include_trajectory` on only logs that
no trajectory is available. If your pipeline *depends* on those coordinates, set
`require_trajectory=True` so a missing trajectory raises an error instead of producing a
table without those columns.

### Destriping and bad channels

| field | default | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `lf_k_filter` | `False` | Spatial-filter mode for LF destriping. `None` disables LF spatial filtering entirely |
| `skip_lf_destripe` | `False` | Skip LF destriping altogether, for LF that is already preprocessed and decimated (lfpack archives, arrays). Channel labels then come from the source's channel table |
| `channel_labels` | `None` | Explicit per-channel bad-channel labels, overriding automatic detection |
| `extra_kwargs` | `{}` | Passed straight through to the underlying engine |

By default the calculator resolves channel labels automatically — from stored labels, from
the `.cbin` metadata, or by detecting them on the snippet. Pass `channel_labels` to
override that. To **disable** bad-channel handling completely, pass an all-zero array:

```python
import numpy as np

options = FeatureComputationOptions(
    features_to_compute=["lf"],
    channel_labels=np.zeros(384),   # every channel treated as good
)
```

That is useful when comparing against an external pipeline that does no bad-channel
rejection, or when debugging a suspicion that detection is discarding good channels.

## Per-feature parameters

`feature_params` reaches inside individual feature families. It accepts either the typed
objects or an equivalent nested dict — these two are the same:

```python
from ephysatlas.feature_calculators import CsdParams, FeatureParams

FeatureParams(csd=CsdParams(scale=False))
{"csd": {"scale": False}}
```

Only what you set changes; every other parameter keeps its default, and the default
`FeatureParams()` reproduces the standard output exactly.

::: {.callout-tip}
A misspelled name raises an error: an unknown family name raises `ValueError` and an
unknown sub-parameter raises `TypeError`. The typed objects also let your editor catch it
before you run the code.
:::

### LF parameters — `LfParams`

| field | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `bands` | `None` | Frequency bands for the LF spectral step. `None` uses the standard delta/theta/alpha/beta/gamma set |
| `decay_features` | `True` | Compute the PSD-decay (spectral parameterisation) features. The `csd` family never computes them on its CSD and BPR traces |
| `compute_rms_no_car` | `False` | Also emit `rms_lf_no_car` — LF RMS destriped *without* common-average referencing |

```python
from ephysatlas.feature_calculators import LfParams

options = FeatureComputationOptions(
    features_to_compute=["lf"],
    feature_params=FeatureParams(lf=LfParams(compute_rms_no_car=True)),
)
```

`rms_lf_no_car` is opt-in because CAR removes shared signal across channels; the no-CAR
RMS retains it, which is informative for some analyses and misleading for others.

### CSD parameters — `CsdParams`

| field | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `bands` | `None` | Frequency bands for the CSD spectral step |
| `decimate` | `10` | Temporal decimation applied before computing the CSD. `1` skips it |
| `scale` | `True` | Scale the spatial differences by the tissue conductivity and the intercontact distance (A/m³ for CSD, A/m² for BPR). `False` keeps the raw differences in V |
| `denoise` | `True` | Apply the Cadzow denoiser to the decimated LF before the CSD and BPR finite differences. Turn it off for LF that is already Cadzow-denoised, so it is not denoised twice |
| `cadzow_kwargs` | `None` | Overrides of the Cadzow parameters. `None` uses `features.cadzow_lfp_kwargs(geometry)`; `fs` and `h` cannot be overridden |

LF-only sources whose LF is already decimated and denoised need
`CsdParams(decimate=1, denoise=False)`; see
[computing features from the archives](load-lfp-features.qmd#computing-features-from-the-archives).

```python
options = FeatureComputationOptions(
    features_to_compute=["csd"],
    feature_params={"csd": {"scale": False}},
)
```

The Cadzow defaults depend on the probe layout. `cadzow_lfp_kwargs` returns the
ibl-neuropixel LFP defaults: Gavish-Donoho shrinkage (`shrinkage=2.25`) on the full
lateral × depth grid (`fill_grid=True`) for the NP1 checkerboard, and `shrinkage=1.22`
without grid filling for NP2, whose contacts already fill their grid. To see what a
geometry gets, or to use the adaptive rank cut instead of the shrinkage:

```python
import neuropixel
from ephysatlas.features import cadzow_lfp_kwargs

print(cadzow_lfp_kwargs(neuropixel.trace_header(version=1)))
# {'fill_grid': True, 'rank': 5, 'niter': 1, 'fmax': None, 'nswx': 64, 'ovx': 32,
#  'ppca_k': 2.0, 'shrinkage': 2.25}

rank_cut = CsdParams(
    cadzow_kwargs={"fill_grid": False, "shrinkage": None, "gap_threshold": 2.0, "fmax": 125}
)
```

Changing the Cadzow parameters changes every `*_csd` and `*_bpr` value, so the output no
longer matches the published models.

### Waveform parameters — `WaveformParams`

These are [DARTsort](https://github.com/cwindolf/dartsort) detection parameters, and they need the `[full]` extra.

| field | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `n_jobs` | `0` | `0` runs in the main process (CUDA initialised in-process; GPU memory is not freed between calls). `1` runs in a worker subprocess, which frees GPU memory on exit but needs a working multiprocessing environment |
| `detection_threshold` | `4.0` | Peak detection threshold, in units of channel RMS |
| `spatial_dedup_radius_um` | `150.0` | Radius within which only the largest simultaneous peak is kept |
| `positive_temporal_dedup_radius_samples` | `7` | Samples around a trough in which positive peaks are suppressed |
| `residnorm_decrease_threshold` | `3.162` | Minimum residual-norm decrease for a detected spike to be subtracted |

```python
from ephysatlas.feature_calculators import WaveformParams

options = FeatureComputationOptions(
    features_to_compute=["waveforms"],
    scratch_dir="/fast/scratch",
    feature_params=FeatureParams(
        waveforms=WaveformParams(detection_threshold=5.0, n_jobs=1)
    ),
)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Changing `detection_threshold` changes `spike_count` and every waveform-shape feature —
which means the result no longer matches what the published models were trained on. Keep
the defaults if you intend to run a published model over the output.
:::

## Inspecting the destriped data

`get_destriped_snippet` runs the same destriping as `compute_snippet` but stops there, so
you can look at the intermediate voltage without paying for feature computation:

```python
snippet = calc.get_destriped_snippet(window)

snippet.raw.raw_ap      # (channels, samples) raw AP, volts — or None
snippet.raw.raw_lf      # (channels, samples) raw LF, volts — or None
snippet.raw.fs_ap       # AP sampling rate, Hz
snippet.raw.fs_lf       # LF sampling rate, Hz
snippet.des_ap          # destriped AP — or None
snippet.des_lf          # destriped LF — or None
snippet.geometry        # channel geometry used by the destriper
snippet.channel_labels  # bad-channel labels the destriper applied
```

If the features look wrong, plot raw against destriped to see whether destriping is the
cause:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, (ax_raw, ax_des) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 6), sharey=True)
ax_raw.imshow(snippet.raw.raw_lf, aspect="auto", cmap="RdBu_r")
ax_raw.set(title="raw LF", ylabel="channel")
ax_des.imshow(snippet.des_lf, aspect="auto", cmap="RdBu_r")
ax_des.set(title="destriped LF")
plt.show()
```

`get_destriped_snippet` also accepts a `DestripeOptions` to vary `lf_k_filter`,
`ap_k_filter`, `neuropixel_version` and `nshank` for the inspection alone, without
touching your production options.

![A destriped snippet drawn in grey, scaled on the typical channel: AP (first 50 ms) and LF. [Raw and destriped voltage](../visualise/voltage-snippets.qmd) has the code, the destriping steps and the bad-channel figure.](../figures/destriped_snippet_ap_lf.jpg){.lightbox}

## Provenance

Every feature file written carries the run's provenance in its pandas `.attrs` — package
versions and the parameters used:

```python
print(result.provenance)

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_parquet(result.snippet_level_dir / "lf_features.pqt")
print(df.attrs)
```

This is how you establish, months later, which parameters produced a table on disk. When
`skip_saved_computation` reuses a cached family, its file keeps the provenance of the run
that originally created it — so a mixed directory records the provenance of each part separately.
